body.text: Latin America and the Caribbean’s maritime connectivity is increasingly exposed to the combined effects of climate shocks, geopolitical disruptions, and vulnerabilities across critical shipping corridors
Image Source: Getty Images
This is part of the essay series: Sagarmanthan Edit 2026.

Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC) is a region that exports food and imports the fertilisers required to produce it; that exports energy and imports manufactures; that depends critically on the Panama Canal - one of the most strategically significant chokepoints in the global maritime system, whose operational capacity is structurally conditioned by extreme climate phenomena - and is home to some of the most vulnerable SIDS on the planet. Alongside this main corridor, three north-central Caribbean passages articulate traffic between the Gulf of Mexico, the North Atlantic, and the eastern Caribbean: the Florida Strait, the Windward Passage, and the Yucatan Channel. Their vulnerability - at once climatic, geopolitical, and logistical - when examined as an integrated system, defines the risk architecture underpinning the region's maritime security.

LAC faces, for the first time in decades, the convergence of multiple simultaneous disruptions to its maritime system, equally geopolitical and climatic in nature. The 2023-2024 drought, associated with the El Niño phenomenon, subjected the Panama Canal to the most severe operational crisis in its recent history. The year 2023 was the driest on record in the Canal's watershed, with Lake Gatún - an essential freshwater source for the operation of the locks - reaching unprecedented minimum levels. Daily transits fell gradually but persistently, from the usual average of 35-38 vessels to 22 by December. At the Neopanamax locks, the maximum draft allowed was temporarily reduced from 50 to 44 feet, constraining the cargo capacity of the largest vessels. The Canal only recovered its full operational schedule of 36 daily transits in September 2024. Since 2026, the Panama Canal Authority has implemented preventive water-conservation measures in anticipation of a possible new El Niño episode, thereby acknowledging climate variability as a structural constraint.

Between 2022 and 2024, the Caribbean experienced an increase in average ocean temperatures, a higher frequency and intensity of hurricanes, prolonged droughts, and flooding. Hurricane Beryl illustrated this trend forcefully: it developed from a tropical depression into a hurricane of substantial category - with winds exceeding 160 miles per hour - within just 42 hours, destroying 90% of the mangroves of Union Island. NOAA reported unprecedented sea surface temperatures that acted as a catalyst for rapid intensification. Climate science indicates that climate change has increased hurricane wind speeds by 10% and doubled the probability of rapid intensification of storms. Besides destroying coastal and port infrastructure, this acceleration directly obstructs maritime transport services, undermining food and energy security in island economies. The Caribbean has recorded a 9% decline in its maritime connectivity index over the past decade, a combined result of the concentration of the shipping market and recurrent damage to port infrastructure from extreme climate events.

These impacts transcend physical destruction and have a direct impact on maritime supply chains, increasing insurance costs and freight volatility, and forcing operational diversions. For the region's economies, the sustained loss of connectivity conditions regional trade, makes the import of essential goods more expensive, and weakens overall economic resilience, placing port adaptation as a strategic public policy priority.
A region whose maritime connectivity has been weakened by the intensification of hurricanes possesses a reduced capacity to absorb disruptions in the supply corridors of strategic inputs.

Since March 2026, the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz has tightened the supply of fertilisers with direct repercussions on regional agriculture. Brazil imports approximately 92 percent of its fertilisers; the entire region 85 percent. In this context, climate vulnerability and geopolitical fragility do not operate as independent factors: a region whose maritime connectivity has been weakened by the intensification of hurricanes possesses a reduced capacity to absorb disruptions in the supply corridors of strategic inputs.

In the western hemisphere, three corridors of the north-central Caribbean (the Florida Strait, the Windward Passage and the Yucatan Channel) concentrate the pressure on chokepoints with characteristics that the specialised literature has not yet examined in a fully integrated manner. Their singularity lies in the fact that the vulnerability of these passages is simultaneously climatic and geopolitical.

The Florida Strait, approximately 150 km at its narrowest point, channels traffic between the Gulf of Mexico and the North Atlantic. Its location makes it particularly susceptible to the entry routes of Atlantic tropical hurricanes into the Gulf of Mexico, a corridor that climate models project will be traversed by storms of greater intensity in the coming decades. The Windward Passage, 80 km wide, connects the natural exit from the Panama Canal with the eastern seaboard of the United States via the shortest available route; more than 8,000 commercial vessels use it annually, with trade at risk estimated at 6.52 billion dollars per year, a figure that places it among the nine most vulnerable passages in the world. The coastlines bordering this corridor record some of the highest climate-disaster exposure indices in the hemisphere. The Yucatan Channel, 217 km wide, articulates commerce between northern South America, Central America, south-eastern Mexico and Gulf ports - with trade at risk of 1.99 billion dollars annually - and is likewise a frequent transit corridor for cyclonic systems forming in the Caribbean Sea before entering the Gulf of Mexico.

Nearly 22 million people in the Caribbean live less than six metres above sea level, and most islands have more than half of their infrastructure within 500 metres of the coastline. This physical exposure leads to extreme climate events directly disrupting the operational capacity of the ports and terminals that sustain connectivity across the sub-region. In the face of this severe exposure, overcoming vulnerabilities requires deepening the prospective debate on cross-border regional cooperation schemes and maritime governance reforms.

Strengthening infrastructure resilience involves modernising port assets with climate adaptation criteria, coordinating the management of strategic passages, and building institutional frameworks capable of sustaining the continuity of trade flows in the face of concurrent crises.

Ultimately, strengthening the resilience of the region's maritime corridors will require treating connectivity not only as a logistical concern, but as a strategic foundation of regional economic and food security.

The governance of these corridors is not conditioned solely by bilateral tensions between the United States and Cuba, but by the broader geopolitical alignments of a shifting international order and by the growing weaponisation of maritime infrastructure as a national and economic security asset by multiple powers, a process known as the securitisation of maritime space. This set of challenges merits further research and discussion on possible paths for future decision-making, addressing multiple dimensions, among which the following are preliminarily proposed:

• Adaptive infrastructure and resilience standards: Define mandatory regional adaptive design criteria for the shielding and elevation of critical port infrastructure in vulnerable island nodes and terminals.

• Regional governance and cooperation: Establish a Maritime Corridor Coordination Table in the Wider Caribbean for the exchange of operational data and coordinated responses to chokepoint closures or climate disasters.

• Logistical and input contingency mechanisms: Create shared strategic reserves and alternative cabotage routes for critical inputs such as fertilisers, food, and fuels, reducing reliance on exposed corridors.
Ricardo J. Sánchez is an economist with a PhD in Economics and more than 35 years of professional experience in infrastructure planning and specialised advisory services in transport and logistics.
